textbookText: • Digitigrade locomotion: found in tiger, leopard, cat, dog, wolf etc. in which only digits touch on ground at running and digits are with shock absorbing pad on the ventral surface.
• Unguligrade locomotion: found in cow, goat, horse etc. in which animals move on tips of hoofed toes.
• Plantigrade locomotion: found in bear, primates etc. where the entire palm or sole of feet touch on ground while running.

b. Fossorial adaptation: Animals which are adapted to live underground by making burrows or holes are called fossorial animals. Such adaptation is known as fossorial adaptation. These animals come out of burrow mostly at the night time in search of food and other activities. Example: moles, burrowing owls, some rodents, badgers etc.

Figure: 9.1.4 Fossorial adaptation i. Their body is compact, rigid and spindle shaped. ii. Head is anteriorly tapered to form somewhat conical snout that aids in digging. iii. Shoulder muscles are powerful and well developed. iv. Forelimbs are short, stout, provided with claws and shovel like palms. Example: mole Biology, Grade 11 | 435

v. Tail is either absent and if present, found in reduced form. vi. Eye and external ears are poorly developed. Eyes are protected by nictitating membrane. In some forms external ears are totally absent (spiny ant eater). vii. Mostly, they undergo hibernation.

c. Arboreal adaptation: Animals adapted for climbing trees, walls, rocks, ceilings etc. are called arboreal animals. This type of adaptation is also called scansorial adaptation. Such adaptation helps them to procure food and also provide retreat and safety. Some arboreal animals permanently live in trees, swing on tree branches and are frugivorous. Arboreal animals can be broadly categorized as: i. Rock and wall climbers: They climb on walls of buildings, rocks. Example: wall lizard, gecko etc. ii. Terrestrio-arboreal form: These animals mostly live in trees and sometime come to the ground. Example: Sloth bear, striped palm squirrel etc. iii. Arboreal form: They are completely tree dwelling forms. Example: Lemur, Gibbon etc.

Figure: 9.1.5 Arboreal Adaptation Following are the arboreal adaptational features: i. They have small, slender and stout body which favors running while climbing walls, rocks, trees etc. ii. Presence of neck provide mobility for head to see object at the vicinity. iii. Their body is covered by dry horny scales which protect the body and also prevents loss of water. iv. Tongue is long, protrusible and sticky for capturing prey. v. The ribs of arboreal animals are curved which give thorax a sub-circular shape. vi. Girdle bones (pectoral girdle and pelvic girdle) are strong enough to support body weight. vii. Their digits have sharp long and curved claw. Some animals like gibbon, orangutans have opposable and prehensile toes in hind feet for climbing and grasping tree branches.

viii. Tail is long and prehensile in majority of the arboreal animals. Flying squirrels have non-prehensile tails provided with spines and scales to prevent from slipped down while climbing. ix. Adhesive lamellas are present on the ventral surface of digits in wall lizard which create partial vacuum to cling on the wall and ceilings. Wall lizard and some geckos can easily detach their tail to escape from predator and later re-grow their tail. x. Adhesive pads are found either at the tip or under surface of tree frog and some geckos. d. Volant/ aerial adaptation:

The adaptation which is shown by the animals to fly or glide in air is called flying or volant adaptation. Some animals fly in air for long time whereas some fly for short duration. None of the aerial animals fly indefinitely, and they have to return to the earth for resting and nesting. Volant adaptation is of two types: 1. Active flight: In active flight, animals fly in air for a long time. This is also called true and sustained flight. Example: Majority of birds, bat and insects.
